title: Do people keep right in a two-way corridor, and which robot passing policy keeps their lanes?
lede: research programme: do people keep right in a two-way corridor, and what do robots do to their lanes? In two Jülich experiments people with no exit instruction walked on their own right 92 to 94% of the time (HERMES 2009, BaSiGo 2013), and an exit instruction cut that to 0.53 and 0.69; when BaSiGo added information on screens, 99.5% kept right despite the exit instruction; on real city pavements head-on passers kept right only 65% of the time in Zurich and 68% in Nicosia; a social-force crowd twin (JuPedSim) fitted to the free-choice runs kept 0.78 on their right under assigned exits where people kept 0.54, so it over-trusts the convention; moving the exits to the walls only lowers that to 0.68, and a second model family, JuPedSim's anticipation velocity model, keeps 0.996 on their right; a bias that switches off when a walker's exit is on its left, with nothing refitted, brings social force to 0.61 and a third family, the collision-free speed model, to 0.62, while the anticipation model stays at 0.88; a fourth family from another code base, the anticipatory power law, keeps 0.97 with the bias always on and 0.70 with the yielding bias, so the over-trust replicates in all four and the fix works in two; a fifth, ORCA (an RVO2 port), keeps 0.88 with the bias always on and 0.60 with it yielding, so the fix works in three of five, and not only where the fitted bias is weak; with robots as 5 to 20% of the agents in three of those crowd models, a robot holding the side opposite the people's convention is the worst passing policy in every model (up to 0.63 of its passes within 0.5 m of a person and 4 s of delay per person), but the models disagree on which of the other three policies is best; adding ORCA (with ORCA-driven robots) and the power law, the three models that passed the held-out test rank all four policies identically by close passes (crowd side, adapt, lateral goal, opposite; Kendall tau 1.00) but not by human delay; a confirmatory rerun with fresh seeds holds it: tau 1.00 with a 95% bootstrap interval of [1.00, 1.00], also at half the keep-right bias, while the delay ranking still disagrees; a small policy learned in any one twin (CEM) holds the crowd's side near the wall and beats every hand policy in all three, and the one trained in social force is the weakest even there; a density-matched control then shows that an apparent speed-up from crowd-side robots in a weak-convention crowd was 88% lower density, not lane seeding; a registered rerun with a same-bodies control (robots walking to a lateral goal) finds the robots' side is what matters: holding the crowd's side gives people 0.12 to 0.21 more lane order and 1.8 to 3.6 s shorter transits than the same robots without it; a 2 x 2 factorial on the robot then shows a crowd-side robot costs people less than the person it replaces in all three twins (0.04 to 0.78 s per transit), that its lane line, not its 1.2 m/s cap, carries that, and that the twins' disagreement is the cost of any extra body (0.28 to 1.88 s); on the real HERMES curve an extra walker costs 0.30 to 0.76 s per 20% at the twins' densities, which the twins mis-price by up to 7x.
summary: An open research programme on which passing policy a fleet of mobile robots should use in a corridor shared with people, with the crowd models fitted to real trajectories and cross-checked across model families (social force, ORCA, the anticipatory power law). Milestone 1 measures the human baseline in the Forschungszentrum Jülich HERMES bidirectional corridor experiments (2009; 24 runs; 4,752 walkers tracked at 16 fps; DOIs 10.34735/ped.2009.10–12). With no instruction about the exit, 1,016 of 1,084 walkers (0.937, two-stage bootstrap 0.865 to 0.993) walked on their own right, both streams on the same relative side, and lane order was 0.91 to 1.00 against 0.25 to 0.52 for shuffled directions. When each walker was told to leave by the left or right exit, the share fell to 0.534 (0.503 to 0.568) over 13 symmetric runs and 0.526 over the asymmetric set, and lanes persisted at lower order (0.59 to 0.85, above the null in every run). Three of five registered predictions held; the share did fall at the highest density (0.82) and the free-speed run walked at 1.73 m/s, above the predicted range. Milestone 2 replicates this on the independent BaSiGo corridor experiment (2013; 15 runs; 8,155 walkers; 4 m corridor; DOI 10.34735/ped.2013.5) with predictions registered first: with no exit instruction 0.924 (0.877 to 0.973) kept right, inside the HERMES interval; with exits assigned by wristband it fell to 0.689 (0.566 to 0.839; difference +0.235, 0.073 to 0.365), a smaller collapse than at HERMES, stepping down at the instruction rather than drifting with run order. In the last two runs, with the exit instruction kept and ‘screen information’ added (content not documented by the archive), 1,212 of 1,218 walkers (0.995) kept right. All six registered predictions held; lane order beat the null in all 15 runs. Milestone 7 checks the convention outside the lab with a head-on encounter measure on the ETH/Hotel (Zurich) and UCY Zara (Nicosia) pavement recordings, after projecting every track back onto its video frames to fix each frame’s handedness: walkers kept right in 0.654 (0.592 to 0.741; 723 encounters) of Zurich passes and 0.680 (0.565 to 0.797; 491) of Nicosia passes, though Cyprus drives on the left; the same measure reproduces the lab’s 0.935 and 0.526. The street convention is real but far weaker than the corridor’s, and two scenes per city cannot separate a city norm from scene layout. Limits: ‘right’ assumes the archive frame is right-handed with z up; neither experiment randomised run order, so the instruction effect is descriptive, and what the BaSiGo screens showed is unknown; laboratory crowd of students; no robots yet. Milestone 3 fits a social-force twin (JuPedSim 1.4.2, Helbing–Farkas–Vicsek parameters, plus one steering bias toward one’s own right when someone approaches head-on) on the nine free-choice runs. Without the bias it keeps 0.51 right; the fitted bias (β = 0.1) gives 0.89 to 0.97 and lane order within 0.10 in 7 of 9 runs, but only 3 of 9 runs fall inside their intervals and the twin cannot congest past about 1.5 walkers/m² (the densest real run reached 3.8). On the 14 assigned-exit runs it never saw it keeps 0.78 on the right where people kept 0.54 (HERMES 3.6 m, pooled), overstating every run: the twin over-trusts the convention. Geometry (corridor length, exit positions) is assumed, as the archive was unreachable this session. Milestone 4a tests that: moving the assigned walkers’ exits from a quarter width in to the walls lowers the held-out share to 0.68, still above people in 13 of 14 runs, and a second family, JuPedSim’s anticipation velocity model (Xu, Chraibi and Seyfried 2021, default parameters), fitted the same way (β = 0.35), forms near-perfect lanes, fails H3 (4 of 9 runs in interval, densities unreachable) and keeps 0.996 on the right under assigned exits. In both families a side bias fitted on free-choice runs survives the goals that made people drop it. Milestone 4b tests the rule rather than the model: a bias that switches off for a walker whose exit lies on its left (walkers without a lateral goal, the only ones in the fitted runs, are unaffected, so nothing is refitted) cuts the mean held-out share error from 0.210 to 0.079 for social force, from 0.353 to 0.118 for a third family, JuPedSim’s collision-free speed model (Tordeux, Chraibi and Seyfried 2016; β = 0.2), and from 0.395 to 0.260 for the anticipation model. Pooled HERMES held-out share: 0.610, 0.623 and 0.877 against people’s 0.541. The collision-free speed model with the yielding bias is the only pair that also gets the held-out lanes (12 of 14 within 0.10). The rule was chosen after the earlier failures were seen, and no rule reproduces the run-to-run spread. Milestone 4c adds a fourth family from another code base, the anticipatory power law of Karamouzas, Skinner and Guy (2014), implemented in numpy with Inria UMANS’s closed-form force and parameters (k = 1.5, τ0 = 3 s; checked against a finite-difference gradient). Fitted the same way (β = 0.35) it keeps 0.971 on the right under assigned exits with the bias always on and 0.698 with the yielding bias (mean error 0.393 → 0.153). The over-trust replicates in all four families; the yielding fix brings the share within 0.10 in the two fitted with β ≤ 0.2, not in the two fitted with β = 0.35 (a pattern seen after the run). The power law fails H3 too, so no family of four reproduces side, lanes and speed-density together, and H3 is refuted. A fifth family, ORCA (optimal reciprocal collision avoidance, ported from RVO2 with UMANS parameters), needs the strongest bias (β = 1.0) and fits the free runs worst, keeps 0.878 with the bias always on and 0.600 with the yielding bias (mean error 0.312 → 0.086, lanes within 0.10 in 11 of 14). So the over-trust replicates in all five families, the yielding fix works in three, and the registered test of the β-strength pattern refutes it. ORCA fails H3 as well. Milestone 5a puts robots in the three JuPedSim crowds (free choice, two HERMES runs, 20 seeds per cell): robots of the people’s size capped at 1.2 m/s (the MiR250’s lower rated speed) replace 5, 10 or 20% of the agents, with four passing policies. A robot holding the side opposite the crowd’s convention is the worst policy on close passes (clearance under 0.5 m), delay per pass and lane order in all nine family-share cells; at 20% it costs people 3.98 s per 8 m transit in social force, 2.05 s and 0.45 s in the other two families, with 0.58, 0.16 and 0.63 of its passes close. A robot holding the crowd’s side keeps close passes at 0.10 or below in every family and leaves the people’s side share within 0.03. The order of the three reasonable policies (crowd side, follow the local majority, a lateral exit goal) differs between families (Kendall τ 0.00 to 1.00), so the H5 preview fails: a policy tuned in one simulator need not rank the same in another. Five of eight registered predictions were refuted. Robots use the crowd’s own operational model, so people can push them. Milestone 5b adds robots to ORCA (the robots run ORCA too) and the power law. The three families that passed the held-out share test (social force, collision-free speed, ORCA) rank the four policies identically by close passes at every share (crowd side < adapt < lateral goal < opposite; Kendall τ 1.00 in 9 of 9), with 0.02 to 0.08 of crowd-side passes and 0.58 to 0.74 of opposite-side passes under 0.5 m at 20% robots. By human delay per pass they disagree (τ 0.00 to 1.00), so H5 holds on one metric and fails on another. Milestone 6a registers H5 on close passes as a confirmatory test: 20 fresh seeds per cell (3,120 runs), the three families at their fitted bias and at half of it. The ranking is identical in all 18 pair-share cells (τ 1.00; 95% bootstrap interval [1.00, 1.00] at the fitted bias), while by delay per pass it fails again (2 of 9 cells at τ ≥ 0.8). Halving the bias moved only the social-force crowd toward the street convention (0.95 → 0.80 on own right), so the weaker-convention check is strong for one family. Milestone 6b trains a five-parameter lateral policy (not SARL) by the cross-entropy method in each of the three twins on equal budgets and evaluates all seven policies on fresh seeds: every learned policy holds the crowd's side harder than the hand-written lane, near the wall, and beats all four hand policies in all three twins, including the two it was not trained in (close passes at 10% robots, ORCA 0.019 → 0.006 to 0.009). The policy trained in social force was the weakest of the three even in social force, its noisiest training signal. Close-pass rankings of the seven policies agree across twins (τ 0.81 to 0.90); delay rankings do not (0.33 to 0.52). Walls cost little in the twins, so a real robot's wall clearance is not modelled. Milestone 6c adds a density-matched control: an apparent speed-up from crowd-side robots in a weak-convention crowd was 88% lower density. Milestone 6d registers the remaining lane-order gain with 40 fresh seeds and a same-bodies arm (robots with a lateral goal): in social force, crowd-side robots at 20 to 30% raise people’s lane order by 0.04 to 0.07 against no robots and by 0.12 to 0.21 against lateral-goal robots, which cost people 1.7 to 2.9 s per transit; in collision-free speed any robots slow people against the control (crowd-side by 0.5 to 0.9 s), though side-holding still beats the lateral goal. Milestone 6e runs the same arms in ORCA and sweeps robot speed in collision-free speed (3,040 runs): in ORCA crowd-side robots beat lateral-goal ones by 1.1 to 4.1 s per transit and 0.04 to 0.15 lane order at every keep-right bias from street-like to fitted, so side-holding wins in all three twins; against no robots ORCA, like collision-free speed, has robots slow people (by up to 1 s) with no lane gain. Faster robots do not remove that slow-down (+0.5 s from 1.2 to 2.0 m/s), but they shrink the side’s advantage (0.70 s at 0.8 m/s to 0.12 s at 2.0 m/s). Milestone 6f crosses the robot’s two differences from a person, its lane line and its 1.2 m/s cap, at a fixed agent count (1,920 runs): a crowd-side robot costs people less than the person it replaces in every twin (0.70 s per transit in social force, 0.42 s in collision-free speed, 0.78 s in street-like ORCA), the line carries all of it and the cap none, and the slow-down against the density-matched control is what any extra walker costs, which the twins put at 0.28 to 1.88 s. Milestone 6g measures that cost on the HERMES runs: crossing 8 m takes 5.5 s at 0.35 persons/m² and 11.5 s at 1.85/m², and removing 20% of walkers saves people 0.30 to 0.76 s at the twins’ operating densities; collision-free speed (1.57 s) and street-like ORCA (1.31 s) over-price it 2 to 3×, fitted ORCA (0.08 s) under-prices it, and every twin but fitted ORCA is 2.3 to 3.9 s too slow at a given density, because walker count was calibrated on speed and the twins reach the real speed at about half the real density. Milestone 6h fits each family’s one spacing parameter to that curve (2,400 runs, seven predictions registered first): collision-free speed at time gap 0.3 s and fitted ORCA at time horizon 2 s now match the real time to cross within about 0.5 s from 0.37 to 1.3 persons/m², on fresh seeds and on the eight assigned-exit runs the fit never saw, while social force (2.2 s off) and street-like ORCA (gridlock) cannot be fitted this way. Matching the level does not match the slope: at 0.83/m² the recalibrated twins put the saving from 20% fewer walkers at 0.19 and 0.01 s against a real 0.40 s, and no twin can reach the dense run’s 1.72/m², near 1.3/m², which it read as the entrance rule capping inflow. Milestone 6i tests that reading by moving re-entry 0.3 to 1.2 m behind the corridor end and changing nothing else (1,640 runs, seven predictions registered first): the highest density at the 1.6 m entrance rises from 1.58 to 2.06/m² in collision-free speed and from 1.32 to 1.58 in social force, and not at all in ORCA, which jams on its own above about 120 walkers. In the one twin that reaches the dense run’s density, 20% fewer walkers save +0.66 s [−0.00, +1.45] against a real +0.72 s, but it crosses 1.7 s too fast there and still under-prices the marginal walker at 0.83/m² (+0.13 against +0.37 s), so one spacing parameter cannot fit the whole curve.
